description: SeamlessAlign is a multimodal corpus of automatically aligned speech translations created to support SeamlessM4T. The paper describes it as the largest open dataset for multimodal translation to date, totaling more than 470,000 hours of speech-text and speech-speech alignments across 37 languages, with open-sourced metadata to recreate the corpus.
name: SeamlessAlign
rai:dataBiases: The paper explicitly notes that mining was focused on 37 target languages in the current version, leaving scaling to all 100 languages for future work. It also discusses broader language-resource imbalance, emphasizing that high-resource languages are prioritized in AI development and that the effort seeks to bridge this gap for lower-resource languages.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created by parallel data mining. Starting with 4 million hours of raw audio from a publicly available repository of crawled web data, the authors chunked files into overlapping segments, applied speech language identification, and mined alignments against sentence-segmented text data drawn from NLLB and against English speech to identify translation pairs.
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper notes that some evaluation samples were missing in CVSS, but for SeamlessAlign construction it discusses filtering and thresholding rather than missing observations. It also notes that not all mined data was used for modeling; only a subset with the highest Sonar alignment scores was selected.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consisted of 4 million hours of raw audio originating from a publicly available repository of crawled web data, plus sentence-segmented text data drawn from NLLB.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Document analysis, Software Collection
rai:dataLimitations: The current version focuses mining on 37 target languages rather than all 100 languages of the full system. The paper notes that mining introduces noisy alignments and that optimal thresholding balances dataset size and alignment quality; not all of the 470,000 hours were used for model training, only high-scoring subsets.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: After collection, the dataset construction used over-segmentation to create several overlapping candidate splits of each speech segment, projected speech and text into a shared embedding space, mined nearest-neighbor alignments with FAISS and a margin criterion, and retained pairs above a Sonar threshold of 1.15. For release and downstream training, the paper also describes filtering subsets with the highest Sonar alignment scores.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The paper states that text used the same data sources, cleaning, and filtering steps as NLLB. For audio, the authors deduplicated audio file URLs, downloaded files, resampled them at 16 kHz, filtered non-speech with a bespoke audio event detection model, applied Voice Activity Detection to split audio into shorter segments, ran speech language identification, and created overlapping over-segmented splits.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper argues that datasets and systems built from SeamlessAlign can improve multilingual speech translation, accessibility, and inclusion, especially for people with low literacy, visual impairments, or languages with multiple writing systems. It also warns that misuse, mistranslations, toxicity, bias, and uneven benefits across user groups remain concerns.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended to support speech-to-text translation and speech-to-speech translation mining, training massively multilingual multimodal translation systems such as SeamlessM4T, and allowing the community to rebuild SeamlessAlign and tune thresholds for their own tasks.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Automatic tools used in the dataset construction pipeline include an ECAPA-TDNN speech language identification model, a bespoke audio event detection model, an open Voice Activity Detection model (Silero), Sonar text and speech encoders for shared multilingual embeddings, FAISS for similarity search, and Stopes mining pipelines.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The raw data consists of publicly available speech audio and text collected from the web. The paper notes that although data cleaning was performed, personally identifiable information may not be entirely eliminated from the mined training data.
